Q: What are microplastics doing to hormones during perimenopause and menopause?
A: Microplastics and related chemicals from packaging and ultra-processed foods can interfere with the endocrine system, which matters most when hormones are already shifting. Dr. Fenwax suggests storing food in glass or steel and cutting back on packaged foods as a first, concrete step.

Q: Who is Dr. Oriel Fenwax?
A: Dr. Oriel Fenwax is a synthetic guest, invented for this test fixture. In the episode he is described as an infectious disease physician whose clinical interest is the microbiome, and who changed his own diet after a routine blood test surprised him.

Q: How does a "bad microbiome footprint" cause sugar cravings and make it hard to eat healthy?
A: A gut fed mostly sugar and processed food favors the bacteria that thrive on it, and those bacteria seem to nudge you toward more of the same. Dr. Fenwax explains that the reverse is also true: feed the gut fiber and fermented foods for a few weeks and the cravings ease. A spoonful of raw sauerkraut a day is an easy place to begin.

Q: What is the triathlete bacteria study and what does it mean for midlife women's endurance and energy?
A: Researchers looked at gut bacteria in endurance athletes and found species that turn lactic acid into short-chain fatty acids the body can use as fuel. Dr. Fenwax points out that the same fatty acids also feed the cells lining the gut, which is useful for any midlife body, not just an athlete's.

Q: Do I need a doctor's referral to get my gut microbiome tested, and will insurance cover it?
A: Consumer microbiome tests do not usually need a referral, and insurance rarely pays for them. Dr. Fenwax recommends treating a first result as directional, comparing it with a second independent test before acting on it, and putting diet and fiber ahead of any pill.
